title: Social Engineering: Impersonation
summary: Impersonation is the identity layer of Social Engineering: the adversary adopts the identity of a trusted person or organisation so that a request is judged against the wrong actor. Typical cases are an executive, a colleague, or a third-party vendor whose mailbox is either spoofed or genuinely compromised, which is why attacker-sent mail can arrive from a real, previously reputable address with valid authentication results. Impersonation is normally preceded by reconnaissance such as gathering victim identity and organisation information, and by acquiring domains or display names that substantiate the false identity; one compromised mailbox frequently becomes the launch point against many partner organisations. Detection combines technical and contextual signals: mismatched display name and address, a first-time sender between two organisations, reply-to divergence, and mailbox audit records showing new inbox rules or forwarding after an unexpected sign-in. Requests that fall outside the sender's normal role or history are the strongest indicator.

beginner.definition: Impersonation means an attacker pretends to be someone you trust. They may act as your manager, a colleague, or a supplier. They may also copy a real person's email address or profile. The goal is to make you act because of who you think is asking.
beginner.whyItMatters: People help people they recognise, and the request often looks completely normal. The message may come from a real account that was taken over. Your filters and your instinct both say it is fine. This is the core of many payment fraud cases, where money is sent to a new account. A single taken-over mailbox can be used to trick many partners.
howItWorks: The attacker learns who you trust by reading public profiles and past emails.
They copy that person's name, title, and signature in their message.
They may register a lookalike domain, or take over the real mailbox instead.
They start with small, friendly messages so you accept the conversation.
Then they make the real request, often a payment or a data share.
They stay in the thread, and may repeat the trick against your contacts.
beginner.example: Imagine a post office counter where a stranger stands in line with a parcel. He greets the clerk with the name of a regular courier, wears a similar jacket, and uses the same words. The clerk stamps the form without checking the badge. The parcel moves on, and the real courier knows nothing about it.
takeaways: Display names are easy to fake, so check the full email address and domain.
A message from a real colleague can still be malicious if their account was taken over.
Call the person on a known number before acting on money or data requests.

objectives: Explain how impersonation differs from the wider parent technique Social Engineering.
Describe why a compromised mailbox makes impersonation more convincing than spoofing.
Identify the reconnaissance activities that usually precede an impersonation campaign.
Recognise header and mailbox artefacts that reveal a false or misused identity.
Explain why verification through a second, known channel stops this technique.
